newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss 1997 budget passes parliament hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Swiss 1997 budget passes parliament hurdle.

text.p: Switzerland's upper house of parliament on Tuesday passed a draft federal budget for 1997 with a deficit of 5.8 billion Swiss francs, slightly higher than a shortfall of 5.7 billion approved by the other chamber.
The spending plan must pass a joint committee of both houses to iron out the differences before it can be adopted as scheduled by mid-December.
The Council of States voted 33 to two for expenditures of around 44.3 billion Swiss francs, about 75 million more than the lower chamber's version approved last week.
The original Federal Council (cabinet) draft foresaw spending of 43.9 billion and revenue of 38.4 billion for a deficit of 5.5 billion.

The main difference between the cabinet and parliament versions is an extra 450 million for unemployment insurance adopted by deputies as it became claer that joblessness could hover near five percent due to a stagnent economy.
The 1996 deficit is budgeted at 4.05 billion but Berne has said nine-month data indicated the actual gap could be 500 million to one billion francs wider.
Parliament also approved a measure empowering the cabinet to borrow about 500 million Swiss francs for additional spending it can release during the year if Swiss economic growth is too slow.

The 1997 budget is based on government projections of 1.5 percent real economic growth and the deficit could swell as high as seven billion if the economy remains stagnant next year, Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger said last month.
The government forecast for the economy, which has contracted for six consecutive quarters, is at the high end of analysts' expectations, which have turned increasingly bearish.

The Swiss National Bank sees gross domestic product rising 1.0 to 1.5 percent next year after shrinking an estimated 0.5 percent in 1996. GDP rose 0.1 percent in 1995. -- Zurich Newsroom, +41-1-631 7340
